newsitem.title: UK: Reuters poll sees good odds for EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Reuters poll sees good odds for EMU start.

text.p: The chances of Europe's single currency going ahead on time stand at 72 percent, according to a Reuters poll of market makers, economists and political analysts conducted on Monday in the aftermath of the French election.

The mean of forecasts from 40 contributors across Europe showed that the likelihood of European economic and monetary union (EMU) going ahead on time on January 1, 1999 was still more likely than not, despite a Socialist victory in French parliamentary elections.
The 72 percent average likelihood in Monday's poll compares with the 82 percent figure in the most recent of a regular series of EMU polls, published by Reuters on May 14.
Analysts said that despite a volatility in sentiment over the past couple of weeks, political willpower for EMU should still win the day.
"We feel EMU will still go ahead, but the uncertainty has increased," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi.
"The uncertainty comes from the type of policies pursued and whether France will meet the budget deficit criteria as laid down in the Maastricht Treaty," he said.
The new socialist government in France, elected on Sunday, has promised to address historically high unemployment rates by stimulating domestic consumption.
It has also said it will renegotiate one of the key economic yardsticks for joining EMU -- bringing the budget deficit to three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP).

France's attempts to reinflate the economy may cause problems for Germany, already under fire for plans to revalue gold reserves which will bring the country's total debt to GDP ratio down below the required 60 percent and help to meet the Maastricht criteria.
But analysts said Chancellor Helmut Kohl was determined that EMU should start on time because the chances of delay becoming a cancellation were too great.

"Germany is suspected of being willing to allow a flexible interpretation of the criteria, this is the main reason we still believe EMU will start in 1999," said Soeren Nielsen, area manager at Jyske Bank in Copenhagen, Denmark.

A flexibile interpretation of the Maastricht criteria to accommodate France and Germany would probably mean that countries such as Spain, Italy and Portugal would have a better chance of joining at the start, the analysts said.
Thirty out of 40 contributors saw the prospect of a softer euro after the French election, as quite likely or very likely.

"The French socialists win means that a large majority voted against the belt tightening. One of the two central partners in EMU has said they they don't want to be ready for the euro in 1999 at at any cost," said Paul Horne, chief international economist at Smith Barney France in Paris.
Seven were neutral and three said a soft euro would not necessarily be the result of a wider membership.

"Central bankers are central bankers and they will want a strong currency. The European Central Bank will be independent and all countries will be represented," said Heidi Sherman, senior economist at the IFO institute in Germany. "Most of those countries want a strong European currency."
A majority of 37 contributors said they it was very unlikely EMU would go ahead without France and three said it was fairly unlikely.
"Germany and France are the strongest economies in Europe and starting without them is not possible," said Raents Abma, economist at the Dutch employers' federation VNO-NCW.
